title: Cicero sets him on fire (3.4)
hook: a book of philosophy makes him long for wisdom itself
tomorrow: what did his mother see in her dream?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Carthage: a cauldron of unholy loves, and a young man who loved to love. The line was carthage, a heat named honestly.

Required reading. The book you skim for the test and forget by summer. Augustine had one of those. He was training to be a public speaker, and his course set a book by Cicero, the Roman orator, to study for its style. He read it for the sentences. Then the book did something nobody assigned. It changed what he wanted.
screen: `REQUIRED READING.` → `CICERO, FOR THE STYLE.` → `IT CHANGED WHAT HE WANTED.`

segments.voice: The book was the Hortensius, urging its reader toward philosophy, and Augustine explains the word: the love of wisdom is what the Greeks call philosophy. The book turned his prayers toward God, he says, and made every empty hope look cheap. He longed, with a burning heart, for a wisdom that doesn't die. What delighted him was that Cicero pushed no single school. Love wisdom itself, wherever it is. One thing cooled him: the name of Christ wasn't in it, a name he'd drunk in, he says, with his mother's milk. So what is the love of wisdom for? Augustine's answer is that it's reaching for a person. Paul names him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Christ the power of God, and the wisdom of God." A neighbor says something close. In the Mishnah, in the sayings called Pirkei Avot, the sage Ben Zoma asks, who is wise? And answers: the one who learns from every person. Augustine caught fire from a pagan's book; Ben Zoma would recognize that kind of learner. And one honest difference. Avot's sayings sit among teachings on studying Torah, and the wisdom it prizes is learned there. For Augustine, the wisdom he longed for turned out to have a name, Christ. Two traditions, each in its own words, both ready to learn from anyone.
screen: `THE LOVE OF WISDOM.` · `ONE NAME MISSING.` · `CHRIST, THE WISDOM OF GOD.` · `BEN ZOMA: LEARN FROM EVERY PERSON.` · then, large: `LONGING FOR WISDOM.`

segments.voice: Find one book on your shelf or your phone that once made you long for something wiser or truer, and look at its cover, or one line from it. Rest your eyes there for a few breaths, then ask, without rushing an answer, what that longing is reaching for.
Cicero sets him on fire. A Roman book of philosophy turns Augustine from style toward the love of wisdom itself, though one name was missing from it.
screen: `CICERO SETS HIM ON FIRE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: longing for wisdom, lit by a book and aimed at someone. I'll be here tomorrow.

chat.says: Mia's reading old Jewish sayings for class: who's wise? someone who learns from everyone. isn't that Augustine?
options: Neighbors, not twins. Ben Zoma says it in Pirkei Avot; for Augustine, wisdom has a name: Christ.
Same thing exactly. Every tradition means one identical wisdom, so the names don't matter.
Not really. Augustine thought you could only learn wisdom from Christian books.
chat.meaning: Shared ground: Ben Zoma's wise person learns from everyone, and Augustine caught fire from Cicero. The honest difference: Avot ties wisdom to Torah; Augustine's longing found its name in Christ.

Hortensius.meaning: Cicero's book urging readers toward philosophy

Mishnah.meaning: an early collection of Jewish teaching on the law

Pirkei Avot.meaning: Sayings of the Fathers, a tractate of wise sayings in the Mishnah

Ben Zoma.meaning: a sage quoted in Pirkei Avot

Torah.meaning: God's teaching; the five books of Moses
